name: Gareth Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes back to your company with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run sales operations for the trade side of a big building-supplies company, the people who sell timber, plasterboard and cement to builders. There are five of us, we handle pricing, quotes and the account data for about three hundred branches. My morning is usually fixing quotes that went out wrong, then I spend the afternoon building little automations so we stop having to fix them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building things that save time, I've got AI helpers doing half our quote checks already. I like that the company lets you try stuff if it makes money. What wears me out is the old managers who think a spreadsheet emailed around is a system, and the fact I'm still learning how to lead people twice my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the five pictures. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the useful bits stay and the hype goes, which is how most things work. I'd post a bit about the automations that actually paid off. At work I'd keep showing results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, even good. I'm the person who gets the time savings, and the company likes savings. My job's safe and I'd probably get promoted for making the team faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building automations and ask for a pay rise based on the savings, maybe ten percent. I'd keep saving about 300 a month. I'd also help my brother Emre with quoting software for his kitchen-fitting business on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty confident, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would helping Emre look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emre fits kitchens and his quotes are on paper. I set up an AI quoting tool for my brother Emre's kitchen business, and it paid for itself in a month. I'd keep doing that kind of thing on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House building's slowed this year, and our trade sales are down a bit. If that keeps going, head office gets trimmed. But I'd be the last one they cut, because I'm the one saving money.

say: The **useful bits stay** and the hype goes, which is how most things work.
I'd keep **showing results** at work and post about the automations that paid off.
think: I'm the one delivering **time savings**, so my job's safe.
I'd probably get **promoted** for making the team faster.
do: Ask for a **ten percent** pay rise based on the savings.
Help my brother with **quoting software** on weekends.
feel: **Calm** and pretty confident that small AI gains work in his favour.

fieldNote: He sees himself as the **beneficiary** of small AI gains.
His only worry is a **house-building slowdown** affecting trade sales.
He already helps his brother's business, a **family side income** in the making.

steps.text: Ask for a ten percent rise based on quote savings
Build more automated quote checks for the trade team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big chance for people who move early, and a warning for those who don't. I'd say it at work in so many words. Online I'd talk about what we've automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I'm already doing the automating, so I'd probably end up running it across the company. The team of five might shrink, but I'd be the one deciding how, which isn't comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch the directors a plan to automate quoting across all three hundred branches, in the first six months. I'd ask for a bigger role and pay. I'd also start a proper side business with Emre, selling quoting tools to small trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. A little guilty about the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Guilty how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because one of my team, Pauline, has done pricing for fifteen years. If I automate pricing across three hundred branches, my colleague Pauline's fifteen years of experience becomes a checkbox. I'd try to move her into customer accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think the side business would work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every small builder I know quotes on paper or in a messy spreadsheet. Emre's mates keep asking him how he does it. It's a gap, and gaps make money.

say: It's a **big chance** for people who move early and a warning for others.
Online I'd talk about **what we've automated**.

The team might shrink, and I'd be **deciding how**.

Ask for a **bigger role** and pay.
Start a **side business** with my brother selling quoting tools.
feel: **Calm** and excited, but **a little guilty** about his team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge, and people need to stop waiting for government to save them. I'd say it at work and online. I'd also say families should stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes too. If AI does any thinking work as well as a person, nobody needs a sales ops manager to run the AI. Emre's kitchen work is hands-on, so it lasts until about 2031, and that's where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into business with Emre properly within six months, doing the quoting, ordering and admin so he can fit more kitchens. I'd keep three months of savings and put the rest into tools and a second van. I'd learn to fit kitchens myself on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but it's a short one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't the quoting and admin side exactly what AI takes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you're right, it is. My brother Emre's kitchen business needs hands more than it needs my spreadsheets, so I'd learn to fit cabinets. The admin would be done by AI anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your girlfriend Nadia say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say go for it, she's a physio, so she's hands-on too. She'd also say don't spend all our savings on a van. She's usually right.

say: People need to **stop waiting** for government to save them.
Families should **stick together**, I'd say at work and online.
think: My job goes too, because nobody needs a **manager to run** the AI.
My brother's **kitchen fitting** lasts until about 2031.
do: Join my brother's business **within six months**.
Put savings into **tools and a van**, keeping three months back.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan, but **a short one**.
S2.quote: My brother Emre's kitchen business needs hands more than it needs my spreadsheets, so I'd learn to fit cabinets.
fieldNote: Even this early adopter expects his **office job to go**.
His plan is **family business**, moving into hands-on work.
He admits his admin role would be **taken by AI** too.

steps.text: Leave sales ops to join his brother's kitchen business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you move now. I'd say it at work, and I'd mean it. Online I'd talk about building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for a few years and build the side business. By 2031 my office role is gone, but I'd have a business by then. Hands-on work lasts until 2034, so the kitchen business has a few years more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business with Emre on the side in the first year, and learn fitting properly. I'd save hard, maybe 500 a month. I'd stay in sales ops while it pays well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. I like a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the kitchen business when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd rather own the business that buys the kitchen robot than be the fitter it replaces. That's the plan for 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn the tools, and to learn something practical. I'd tell them where I'm going. I'd be straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. I'd say it at work and online. I'd be fairly relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could build a proper company, maybe a few vans and staff. My office job would go by 2036, but by then I'd be running a business. Hands-on work lasts until 2039, and I'd plan to buy the robots when they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in sales ops a few years, save, and build the business with Emre. I'd buy a house with Nadia. I'd invest in the business steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. It's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad ran a shop for thirty years, and he'd be proud. My dad always said working for yourself beats working for someone else, and ten years is enough to prove him right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have kids in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably in a few years. I'd want them to grow up seeing a family business. That matters to me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to leave my job and start a business in the same year with almost no runway. What would help is less red tape for small businesses, and banks willing to lend to people starting out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about family businesses. Everyone asks about office jobs, but a brother with a van and a kitchen-fitting business is the best safety net I've got.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about office jobs, but a brother with a van and a kitchen-fitting business is the best safety net I've got.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old sales ops manager** leading five at a building-supplies company.
He uses **AI daily**, builds automations, and favours free markets and family.
He is **calm** in the plateau and Steady Disruption, expecting to gain.
Under fast AGI he plans to join his **brother's kitchen business**.
With more time he aims to **build a company** and buy robots himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have almost no runway to start a business.
